content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper leverages training dynamics (TD) to design deep active learning algorithms. The proposed algorithm uses a prediction module to predict the training dynamic of unlabeled data points. Under various assumptions, the authors provide two theorems showing the advantages of using TD. The authors run experiments on various datasets and show the efficacy of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea of incorporating training dynamics to Entropy and Margin (or more generally deep active learning) seems to be new and interesting. 
2. The authors run many experiments and confirm the efficacy of the proposed method.

Weaknesses:
1. It not clear what is the main contribution of this paper except for incorporating training dynamics into Entropy and Margin (while interesting, this idea seems to be very intuitive). The way of approximating TD and constructing the prediction module seems to largely follow existing works.
2. The theorems provided in Section 2.3.2 are developed under many assumptions, yet the developed results do not seem to be strong enough (e.g., Eq. (11) in the Appendix).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is generally well-written and easy to follow. I suggest the authors to further highlight the novelty of the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper presents some interesting ideas for the active learning community. However, I don't think the results/novelties are strong enough. I am inclined to reject the paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use the averaged model prediction at the output layer of deep neural networks for active sampling. The proposed methodology is motivated by the belief that the training dynamic of the deep learning model is a valid indicator of the uncertainty for unlabeled data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths and weakness:
Strength:
The paper is written and organized in a neat and simple manner, making the key idea easy to understand.
The paper suggests an interesting (but not new) metric to quantify the informativeness of an unlabeled for active sampling, which is the change of behavior during optimization in a t-window. 

Weakness:
The main methodology is not well demonstrated in the active learning problem setting. The fundamental assumptions that are inexplicitly adopted in the paper, such as the training and unlabeled pool share the same joint data distribution(p(x,y), and the initial training set is large enough to reflect the true training dynamics are hardly true for active learning problems.
The active sampling objective is neither well explained nor formalized. The paper claims TD captures the uncertainty of the data. But it is not clear which type of uncertainty it refers to. Even if TD does capture uncertainty well, it is still a gap between adopting the uncertain data for learning and the model improvement. 
Some of the experimental settings
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The proposed method is simple and clear to me. But it is not clear to me why TD is guaranteed to work as some sort of uncertainty measure for active sampling, especially when the actual label of the sample is ignored. In pool-based active learning, The learning of the model is supposed to start with limited training samples. But in this paper, the model starts with abundant training samples and a pretrained network, which are usually unavailable in active learning due to the high annotation cost. 
Also, the proposed method is simply the entropy or margin of the mean predictive distribution for several epochs. I don’t think it even captures the training dynamic well. Suppose p(x1) for three epochs are (0.1,0.9),(0.5,0.5),(0.9,0.1) while p(x2) are (0.5,0.5),(0.5,0.5),(0.5,0.5). If I understand correctly, \bar{p(x1)} and \bar{p(x2)} equals to each other and yield to same TD. But apparently, their training dynamics are different.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The active learning objective is not clearly defined in the paper. 
The novelty of the paper is limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper describes a novel method for active learning which is based on understanding the  training dynamics of the classifier and predicting the TD for the unlabeled set via a prediction module. They use the margin and entropy AL with respect to the training dynamics measurements. The authors provide theoretical justification and experiments where they compare their method with other baselines, including loss prediction, entropy and margin, as other mainstream AL algorithms.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1.	The method seems to be novel and interesting in the sense that following the training dynamics is a new idea, and including a prediction module clearly reduces the need to look explicitly at the unlabeled set dynamics.
2.	The theoretical support is focused and seems to be relevant and helpful to guarantee the methods foundation
3.	Overall the organization and flow of the paper make it and easy and interesting read
Weaknesses
1.	I found the experiments rather confusing. Can the authors explain why they chose to show the relative improvement instead accuracy? Also, what is the definition of the relative improvement, is it with respect to the last query? A simple definition would improve the flow.
2.	The experiments showing the accuracy vs the number of labels show that the difference with other method is quite small in the range of 1-2%
3.	Some of the experiments are stopped too soon when the accuracy curve is still in a sharp slope. It would be interesting if at convergence the TiDal methods indeed reach a higher accuracy then the other methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1.	The method seems to be novel and interesting in the sense that following the training dynamics is a new idea and including a prediction module clearly reduces the need to look explicitly at the unlabeled set dynamics.

3.	Overall the organization and flow of the paper make it and easy and interesting read
content.summary_of_the_review:
In my view the paper is on the borderline for acceptance mainly because of the experiments showing a somewhat dubious improvement, which is not clear if it lingers into the higher reachable accuracy per data set.


Questions
1.	Can the authors explain why they chose to show the relative improvement instead accuracy? Also, what is the definition of the relative improvement, is it with respect to the last query?
2.	Can you please show experiments lingering into the highest accuracy regime (e.g. in figs 10, 11)
3.	Please why is the relative improvement considered a useful metric to show for the superiority of your method? what is the improvement is higher but the overall accuracy is much lower?

content.title: TiDAL: Learning Training Dynamics for Active Learning
content.TL;DR: TiDAL: Learning Training Dynamics for Active Learning
content.abstract: Active learning (AL) aims to select the most useful data samples from an unlabeled data pool and annotate them to expand the labeled dataset under a limited budget. Especially, uncertainty-based methods choose the most uncertain samples, which are known to be effective in improving model performance. However, AL literature often overlooks training dynamics (TD), defined as the ever-changing model behavior during optimization via stochastic gradient descent, even though other areas of literature have empirically shown that TD provides important clues for measuring the sample uncertainty. In this paper, we propose a novel AL method, Training Dynamics for Active Learning (TiDAL), which leverages the TD to quantify uncertainties of unlabeled data. Since tracking the TD of all the large-scale unlabeled data is impractical, TiDAL utilizes an additional prediction module that learns the TD of labeled data. To further justify the design of TiDAL, we provide theoretical and empirical evidence to argue the usefulness of leveraging TD for AL. Experimental results show that our TiDAL achieves better or comparable performance on both balanced and imbalanced benchmark datasets compared to state-of-the-art AL methods, which estimate data uncertainty using only static information after model training.
